items.stem: A provider's host machine has 256 GB of RAM, and 8 GB is kept for the hypervisor. The provider sells 40 guests with 8 GB each. What is the likely result?

options.text: The guests share 248 GB, so they slow down whenever many of them are busy at the same time.
options.feedback: The provider has promised 320 GB and has 248 GB. This works while guests are rarely all busy together. When they are, every guest slows down, which is the noisy-neighbor problem.

options.text: Each guest crashes as soon as it starts, because there is not enough memory for all of them.
options.feedback: Overselling does not stop guests from starting. The memory is promised without being reserved, so the guests run and then compete for it.

options.text: Nothing changes, because every guest has its own separate hardware.
options.feedback: The hardware is shared. The hypervisor divides one physical machine between the guests, so they do compete for it.

options.text: The hypervisor buys more RAM automatically.
options.feedback: A hypervisor only divides the hardware that exists. It cannot add memory.

items.stem: Before you try it: in the cloud setup you provision three servers and then delete two of them. What happens to the bill after that?

options.text: It keeps growing, but only for the one server that is still running.
options.feedback: The cloud bills by the hour for servers that exist. Deleted servers stop costing money, and the remaining one keeps costing ₱3 per hour.

options.text: It stops growing for all three servers, because the setup fee was already paid.
options.feedback: There is no setup fee in the cloud setup. The meter runs for as long as a server exists.

options.text: It keeps growing for all three servers until the end of the month.
options.feedback: That describes a fixed purchase or contract. In this setup the meter stops when you delete a server.

options.text: It drops back to zero, because you released most of your capacity.
options.feedback: The bill never goes down, because you pay for hours already used. It only stops growing for the deleted servers.

items.try: Choose the cloud setup, press Provision a server three times, then press delete on two of them. Watch the Bill so far meter.

items.stem: Before you try it: enlistment opens and thousands of students arrive in the same second. Autoscaling is on and each new machine takes 60 seconds to boot. What happens to requests in that first minute?

options.text: Many are turned away, because the new machines are still booting.
options.feedback: The autoscaler reacts within seconds, but a machine that is still booting cannot serve anyone. A surge that arrives in one second ends before the new capacity does.

options.text: All are served, because autoscaling adds machines instantly.
options.feedback: Autoscaling is fast, but each new machine still needs time to boot.

options.text: None are turned away, because the machines already running can absorb any surge.
options.feedback: The machines running before the surge are sized for ordinary load. A surge many times larger exceeds their capacity.

options.text: The autoscaler cannot detect the surge until it ends.
options.feedback: The autoscaler checks the load every few seconds and orders machines quickly. The delay comes from booting.

items.try: Choose Enlistment, 8:00:00, keep the boot time at 60 s and press Start the day. Then lower the boot time and compare the Turned away figure.

items.stem: Your capstone team forgets a test server over the holidays and receives a bill for it. Which NIST characteristic explains the bill?

options.text: Measured service: usage is metered and billed for as long as the resource exists.
options.feedback: Metering is the reason cloud costs are operational expenses, and the reason a forgotten resource keeps charging you.

options.text: Resource pooling: the provider shares hardware between customers.
options.feedback: Pooling explains why prices are low and why neighbors can slow you down. It does not explain a bill for an idle server.

options.text: On-demand self-service: you create servers yourself.
options.feedback: Self-service explains how the server was created. The charge comes from metering.

options.text: Broad network access: the server can be reached from many devices.
options.feedback: This describes how you connect to the server. It has no effect on billing.

items.stem: Your team first rents a bare cloud server (IaaS) and later moves the same app to a platform such as Railway (PaaS). Who is responsible for installing operating system updates in each case?

options.text: Your team on IaaS, and the provider on PaaS.
options.feedback: On IaaS you receive a virtual machine and run everything above it, including the operating system. On PaaS the provider runs the layers under your code.

options.text: The provider on both, because the servers are in the provider's data center.
options.feedback: The building and hardware belong to the provider on both. On IaaS the operating system is yours to maintain.

options.text: Your team on both, because the app is yours.
options.feedback: On PaaS you push code and the provider runs the operating system and runtime.

options.text: The provider on IaaS, and your team on PaaS.
options.feedback: This reverses the models. The more of the stack the provider runs, the further right you are in the table: IaaS, then PaaS, then SaaS.
